name: Bilal Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. This conversation is confidential. What is your ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Bilal Lopez, 43, fitting stair rails and partitions on a student-housing building site. I have a vocational trade certificate and years in construction, with solid everyday skills; I still ask the lead on an unfamiliar anchor. The contractor pays a typical site wage. I have never used an AI tool, and I care more about a rail passing its pull test than about a faster screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the job support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works steady hours at a preschool. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about four months of bills saved. There are some other builders nearby, though I like this crew because we take checks seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the student-housing crew a faster order sheet might be nice, but the stair rail still has to hold a person. I have never used an AI tool and do not feel behind for that. I want the approved drawing and the right anchors in the box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and can fit ordinary rails and partitions without much fuss. The contractor pays a normal site wage, my partner works steady hours at a preschool, and we have four months of bills saved. There is a mortgage and two school-age children, but our week is fairly predictable at present.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the paid housing shifts and check the first rail anchor with the lead carpenter before repeating the line. In the first year I'd continue putting a small amount into the emergency account each month. I'd also attend the next union safety meeting about anchor testing, which was on the calendar before anyone mentioned AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like the work when a rail feels solid in my hand. A small office saving is not much of a threat to our wages, though I still want the crew paid for its time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did anchor testing settle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One batch looked right in the packet but failed a pull test on the wall. We stopped, got the supplier to replace it and avoided fitting a whole stairwell badly. The rail-anchor pull test on the actual wall was worth the delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the savings account cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four months of ordinary bills if one wage stops, assuming we cut extras. We built it slowly after buying the house. I would rather keep the account than treat it as money for a new kitchen.

say: I would say **faster orders** still leave rail safety to the site crew.
I would insist on **approved anchors** and a real wall test.
think: I am a **certified experienced** worker on a normal site wage.
Four months saved and my partner’s **preschool hours** make current income predictable.
do: Keep paid **student-housing shifts** and test first rail anchors.
Continue monthly **emergency savings** from regular wages.
Attend the **union safety meeting** on anchor testing.
feel: **Calm** about wages while attentive to safety and paid time.
S0.quote: The rail-anchor pull test on the actual wall was worth the delay.
fieldNote: Bilal’s **failed anchor batch** explains his insistence on physical checks despite a tidy order sheet.
A **four-month reserve** and steady preschool wage make the plateau genuinely calm for this household.

steps.text: Keep paid housing shifts and check the first rail anchor
Continue monthly transfers into the household emergency account
Attend the union safety meeting about anchor testing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office may buy anchors and book crews faster, and that could reduce waiting. I would ask for the revised schedule on paper so a worker can check which stairwell is ready. If management uses software to set a faster pace, the union should see the hours and safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on fitting still has a place while robots spread slowly. I do worry that the contractor might stop replacing workers who leave and press us to cover more rails. We have four months saved and some other builders around, so I would not expect my own wage to vanish this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the site manager for a printed weekly stairwell plan and note any unsafe overlap of crews. I'd bring repeated pace problems to the union representative with dates, not rumours. In the first year I'd keep paid shifts and ask two local builders what rail-fitting work they have if our own crew starts losing days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. A better plan could spare us a wasted morning. I would not like a neat screen being used to rush an anchor test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a pace problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we are booked to finish two stairwells in the time one safe pull test takes, I would write down the rooms and hours. Then I would ask the lead what can be done properly. The union needs facts to bargain with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave this crew for another builder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare a real offer, but I like working with people who take rail safety seriously. The mortgage could handle a short gap, not a careless injury. I would ask about both pay and the test procedure before moving.

say: I would ask for a **printed stairwell plan** as booking changes.
I would involve the **union** if software pushes unsafe pace targets.
think: I expect continued **rail-fitting work** while robots spread slowly.
Fewer replacement hires could raise pressure, though my **four-month reserve** protects income near term.
do: Request a **weekly printed plan** and note unsafe crew overlaps.
Take dated **pace problems** to the union representative.
Keep paid shifts and ask **two local builders** about rail work if days fall.
feel: **Uneasy** about pace, while expecting his own wage to continue.
S1.quote: The union needs facts to bargain with.
fieldNote: Bilal accepts faster booking if **pull tests** and safe crew spacing remain possible.
He expects his own **paid work** to continue for now, making unease a closer fit than income anxiety.

steps.text: Keep paid housing shifts while reviewing printed stairwell schedules
Take dated unsafe pace examples to the union representative
Ask two local builders about rail work if current paid days fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers full thinking AI reaches the planning office by 2028, while robots able to fit rails arrive around 2031. I would ask the contractor to show a full stairwell test with people kept clear. A robot rail demonstration that skips the anchor pull test is no demonstration for this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the office changes and 48 when robots can do the hands-on fitting. Four months saved would let us search, but not stop earning, and some local builders may use the same machines. My partner's preschool job should keep its hands-on work until robots too; I cannot call either wage permanently safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid site shifts and ask the union representative to seek a written plan for robot trials and staffing. If the contractor offers paid instruction on checking machine-fitted rails after a real safety trial, I'd attend, though the machine may learn checking as well. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for paid building maintenance work where openings exist and put extra shifts into the emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can ask for written terms and look for another wage, but the 2031 date is close. I would be angry if the contractor announced a machine before explaining what happens to the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why building maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have repaired rails in occupied buildings and know how to talk with people using the stairs. A capable robot could do repairs too, so I see a paid vacancy as time to earn, not a permanent shelter. I would check the actual job notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would paid instruction need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real stairwell, a clear stop control and a supervisor who can sign off the rail. I would not pay for a video course out of our emergency fund. The contractor buying the machine should pay for workers to learn safely.

say: I would tell the crew **2028 office AI** comes before 2031 rail-fitting robots.
I would demand a **full stairwell test** including anchor pull checks.
think: I would be **48** when capable robots can fit rails.
Four months saved allows a search, but **both hands-on wages** may face robots eventually.
do: Keep paid **rail shifts** and seek written robot terms through the union.
Attend **paid safety instruction** if a real trial and supervisor are provided.
Apply for paid **building maintenance** where vacancies exist after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about the 2031 job risk, with several actions available.
S2.quote: A robot rail demonstration that skips the anchor pull test is no demonstration for this job.
fieldNote: Bilal’s focus on the **anchor pull test** links robot safety to a fault he has personally seen.
He views maintenance as **paid work now**, not lasting protection once robots can also do repairs.

steps.text: Keep paid rail shifts while the housing contractor has work
Ask the union for written robot trial and staffing terms
Attend paid machine-rail safety instruction if a real trial is offered
Apply for paid building maintenance vacancies after 2028 if posted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the planning office changes by 2031 and site robots able to fit rails follow around 2034. Five years is enough for a contractor to test a machine on real stairwells and publish what failed. I would ask for paid apprenticeships before older workers leave and their knowledge goes with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I should have even more fitting experience, but at 51 robots could match my hands. The children will be older, yet the mortgage could still run. The longer warning lets us build more savings and ask whether any paid checking or repair jobs actually remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fitting rails and ask the lead to show me more unusual anchor repairs. My partner and I would put overtime into the emergency account until it covers six months, if extra hours come. In the first year after 2031 I'd ask the union for trial results and apply to a paid maintenance opening only if one is posted and the wage covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The current work and pay should continue for several years in this picture. I can use the time to improve and save without pretending a checking job is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would six months change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would give us room to search without touching the children’s school costs immediately. We are at four months now, so it is a reachable goal if overtime returns. I would not count overtime before it is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should teach younger workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Experienced fitters on paid site days, not a screen alone. I have a trade certificate because someone showed me how to test a rail. An apprenticeship needs a safe stairwell and a wage.

say: I would ask for **real stairwell trials** before 2034 rail robots arrive.
I would defend **paid apprenticeships** before skilled workers leave.
think: I would be **51** when capable robots can match my fitting work.
More warning may let us build a **six-month reserve** if overtime appears.
do: Keep paid **rail shifts** and practice unusual anchor repairs.
Put **overtime into savings** until six months of bills are covered.
Ask the **union** for trial results and apply for paid maintenance if posted.
feel: **Uneasy** about the future, while expecting current wages for several years.
S3.quote: An apprenticeship needs a safe stairwell and a wage.
fieldNote: Bilal treats **six months saved** as conditional on paid overtime, not a promise from his current budget.
His call for **apprenticeships** grows from his own certified training and concern about safe rail work.

steps.text: Keep paid rail shifts and practice unusual anchor repairs with the lead
Put paid overtime into savings until six months of bills are covered
Ask the union for published robot trial results after 2031
Apply for a paid maintenance opening if posted after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew office planning changes by 2036 and robots able to fit rails arrive around 2039. A decade gives us time to learn what machines actually do and teach the next group well. I would still insist that every stair rail is pull-tested today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 when robots can do hands-on fitting. The children will be grown, so school fees will not take the same share. The mortgage might be smaller, but I have no reason to assume I can retire at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking paid rail work and ask for supervised repairs on older stairwells. We would build the emergency account toward six months before making extra mortgage payments. In the first year after 2036 I'd watch a real robot trial with the union safety representative and look at local paid roles only if our shifts begin to fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. Ten years is enough time to pay attention and save if the roster stays steady. I cannot control what every builder buys, but I can keep working well now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you prefer to stop work at 56?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would welcome more time with my partner, but we still need wages for ordinary bills. A mortgage paid down would help, not provide an income. I would not call our savings a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a trial convincing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot must fit a rail on a real wall, stop when an anchor fails and leave a record a person can check. The union safety representative should be there, along with the site lead. I would trust a full robot rail test more than a sales film.

say: I would say **2039 rail robots** leave time for real trials and apprenticeships.
I would still insist on **pull tests** today.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and perhaps a smaller mortgage.
Savings are not a **pension**, so paid work may still be needed.
do: Keep paid **rail work** and learn older-stairwell repairs.
Build **six months of savings** before extra mortgage payments.
Watch a **robot trial** with the union safety representative after 2036.
feel: **Calm** near term if the roster and household wages stay steady.
S4.quote: I would trust a full robot rail test more than a sales film.
fieldNote: Bilal uses the long runway for **savings and supervised repairs**, without assuming retirement at 56.
His request for a **union-witnessed trial** follows his earlier failed-anchor experience.

steps.text: Keep paid rail work and practice older-stairwell repairs
Build the emergency account toward six months before extra mortgage payments
Attend a robot trial with the union safety representative after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because capable robots reach rail fitting around 2031 while the children are still in school. A written staffing plan, a complete safety trial and paid training tied to actual work would help. I want the contractor to tell the crew the truth before a machine appears on a stairwell.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a rail after a robot fits it. I have seen a new anchor fail on a real wall despite the box label. The person who signs off that rail has to know what a failed pull feels like.

headlineQuote: The person who signs off that rail has to know what a failed pull feels like.
portrait: Bilal is a **43-year-old certified** construction worker fitting stair rails with experienced, average trade skills.
A typical wage, steady **preschool income** and four months saved support two school-age children and a mortgage.
He has **never used AI** and grounds safety concerns in a real anchor batch that failed a pull test.
He uses the **union** for staffing and trial terms while keeping paid rail work and building savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable rail-fitting robots around 2031 while his children remain school-age.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing plan**, full safety trial and paid instruction tied to work would help.
